sentence: This wall has no open door.
claim: A venule's lining has no ready-made opening for a white cell: neighbouring wall cells meet at closed, regulated junctions, and the leukocyte generates its own micron-scale gap (or a pore through one wall cell) as it squeezes through; this did not need the wall cells to contract (the older view was that the wall cells contract to let it through).
source_title: Barzilai S et al. Leukocytes Breach Endothelial Barriers by Insertion of Nuclear Lobes and Disassembly of Endothelial Actin Filaments. Cell Reports 2017;18(3):685-699 (DOAJ record)
note: Excerpt: 'Leukocytes generate gaps of similar micron-scale size when squeezing through inflamed endothelial barriers in vitro and in vivo ... Gap and pore formation did not require Rho kinase or myosin II-mediated endothelial contractility.' Weizmann coverage: 'Instead of the blood vessel cells contracting to let them through, immune cells squeeze their way through.' Review fix: 'no open door', not 'no door': the seam (c13-c14) is a junction that opens for the cell and closes after it (c26), so the wall has joins but no standing opening. 'This wall' is the frame-0 venule, a continuous lining; the spleen and the marrow's sinusoids work differently, so the line does not say 'your vessels'. Cross-check: Dictionary.com defines diapedesis as passage through 'unruptured walls'; the claim rests on the paper, not the dictionary. The belief the film breaks: the normal makes it a paradox (c5) and the whoa pays it off by name (c16).

sentence: It's a neutrophil, your commonest white cell, about eight micrometres across.
claim: In adults, neutrophils are the most numerous circulating white blood cell: about 60-70% of a normal white count of about 4,000-11,000 cells per microlitre.
source_title: Neutrophilia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (NBK570571)
note: Excerpt: 'In adults, the approximate normal range of white blood cell (WBC) count is 4000 to 11,000 cells/microL, out of which 60% to 70% are mature neutrophils circulating in peripheral blood.' Sources differ on the share (BioNumbers 100511: 60%, range 50-70%, Sell 2001; StatPearls Leukocytosis NBK560882: 40-60%), but neutrophils are the commonest type in every range, so the line says 'your commonest', with no share voiced. Adult ranges: in young children lymphocytes can outnumber them. Replaces the bible's S21 address (statpearls article-31353), which never came up in research. Shares its sentence with c3 (review fix: the size joins this sentence and the red-cell comparison is gone).

sentence: It's a neutrophil, your commonest white cell, about eight micrometres across.
claim: A neutrophil suspended in fluid (round, roughly as in blood) measures about 8.3-8.4 µm across (range about 7.3-9.7 µm), the largest leukocyte type in that study.
source_title: BioNumbers (Harvard Medical School) ID 100510: neutrophil diameter (Downey et al. 1990)
note: Excerpt: '8.4 µm (range 7.3 to 9.7 µm) ... Neutrophils were the largest cells with a mean diameter of 8.3µm'. Isolated cells, measured by Coulter counter and flow cytometry; PMC3605679 gives 7-8 µm, consistent. The bible's 12-15 µm (StatPearls 31353) is a cell flattened on a smear, so the scale pill badges 'round, in blood'. Review fix: 'a little wider than a red cell' is cut (8.3 against a red cell's 7.5-8 µm is within scatter, and the old c4 source only gave the smear value), so c4 is gone. Shares its sentence with c2.

sentence: Yet under a sore fingertip, they pile up outside the wall.
claim: At a site of tissue damage (inflammation), white blood cells move out of the circulation and collect in the damaged tissue, outside the vessels; in a pus-forming lesion those cells are mostly neutrophils.
source_title: How Is Inflammation Involved in Swelling? (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
note: Excerpt: 'Increased blood vessel permeability allows fluid, proteins, and white blood cells to migrate from the circulation to the site of tissue damage.' 'They' are neutrophils: a pathology atlas describes an abscess as 'masses of neutrophils, living and dead' (c19), and PathologyOutlines (skin abscess) a dense infiltrate with many neutrophils. 'Pile up outside the wall' is the cells collecting in that tissue. 'Yet' turns the hook's 'no open door' (c1) into the paradox the film answers. The sore fingertip is spoken here but drawn only once, in the takeaway (review fix): a swelling and a soft glow, no wound or blood, and no colour voiced (redness reads differently on different skin tones). Described as how the body works, with no care advice.

sentence: Rudolf Virchow taught that pus grew from the inflamed tissue.
claim: Virchow and some of his followers held that pus cells arose inside the inflamed tissue's own connective-tissue cells ('connective tissue corpuscles'), not from the blood; in the 1860s this was the accepted theory that Cohnheim's work undermined.
source_title: Cell Pathology (December 1865 report of Dr. Bennett's remarks on Virchow's cell pathology) (PMC9775877)
note: Excerpt: 'the origin of pus-cells, which Virchow and some of his followers had represented as originating in the interior of connective tissue corpuscles'. An exact-phrase search for that sentence returns this page (Bennett disputing the view in 1865), so the row now cites it; PMC6108650, the old source (an 1868 letter), shows no such passage in its visible opening and is dropped, which closes the old 'TODO open link'. Cross-checks: an 1868 review, 'Formation of Pus by Inflammatory Action' (PMC10004891), treats Virchow's view (pus cells from proliferating connective-tissue cells) as the accepted theory Cohnheim's work undermined; an 1873 'Monthly Summary' (PMC6088652) says 'the statement formerly made by Virchow, that the connective tissue is the one source of all inflammatory cells, was too wide'. 'Taught', not 'was wrong': Stricker (1868, PMC10004891) argued that some pus cells still come from tissue. Review fix: 'the inflamed tissue', not 'the injured tissue', since the debate was about inflammation; it simplifies 'its connective-tissue cells'. 'Itself' is gone: 'tissue' against the takeaway's 'blood' carries the contrast. Seen in search excerpts only, so verified_via says so.

sentence: In eighteen sixty-seven, his assistant Julius Cohnheim watched a living frog's vessels.
claim: Cohnheim's first article on inflammation and pus, 'Ueber Entzündung und Eiterung', which reported his frog experiments, appeared in Virchow's Archiv in 1867 (vol. 40, pp. 1-79).
source_title: Cohnheim, Neue Untersuchungen über die Entzündung (1873): Garrison-Morton entry, citing his first article, Virchows Arch. path. Anat. 1867, 40, 1-79 (HistoryofMedicine.com)
note: Excerpt: the entry gives his first article on the subject as 'Virchows Arch. path. Anat., 1867, 40, 1-79' and says he argued, against Virchow, that the essential feature of inflammation is the passage of leucocytes through capillary walls. A 19th-century review (PMC10022970) dates the paper to September 1867, in Virchow's Archives. The Jewish Encyclopedia and Wikipedia give volume 41 (xli); Garrison-Morton's page range points to 40, so the ledger follows it, and the film voices only the year. 'In 1867' dates the published observation; the experiments themselves may have begun earlier. Review fix: the date now rests on the journal citation, not on Wikipedia. The sentence is split from the old three-comma version; 'his assistant' is c24 and the frog is c8.

sentence: In eighteen sixty-seven, his assistant Julius Cohnheim watched a living frog's vessels.
claim: Cohnheim worked under Virchow at the Pathological Institute in Berlin (Britannica: 1865-68; Wikipedia and the Jewish Encyclopedia: assistant from autumn 1864 to 1868), so in 1867 he was Virchow's assistant.
source_title: Julius Cohnheim (Encyclopaedia Britannica, print view)
note: Excerpts (relayed): 'At the Pathological Institute, Berlin (1865-68), Cohnheim was an outstanding pupil of Rudolf Virchow'; while assisting him, Cohnheim also researched the causes of inflammation. Wikipedia: 'Cohnheim became an assistant at Berlin University's pathological institute under Virchow in the fall of 1864, and stayed until 1868.' The start year differs by one between sources; he was in post in 1867 under both, so 'his assistant' holds. No start year is voiced. Review fix: 'his assistant', not 'his own assistant' ('own' is kept once, for the whoa's door).

sentence: In eighteen sixty-seven, his assistant Julius Cohnheim watched a living frog's vessels.
claim: Cohnheim exposed the mesentery of a living frog paralysed with curare ('woorara') and watched its vessels under the microscope.
source_title: Passage of Sanguineous Corpuscles through the Walls of the Vessels, Etc (PMC9799538)
note: Excerpt: 'He demonstrated directly the passage of white and red corpuscles through the vascular walls of the frog mesentery.' The frog was paralysed with 'woorara' (curare), so alive. 'A living frog's vessels' are the vessels of the mesentery, the thin membrane that holds the gut. A translated 19th-century account. Review fix: the sentence has one comma ('his assistant Julius Cohnheim', no apposition commas), so the voice doesn't stutter.

sentence: White cells climbed out.
claim: In Cohnheim's frog, white cells seemed glued to the inside of the vessel wall, pressed into it, lodged in pockets and spread out into the surrounding tissue.
source_title: Passage of Sanguineous Corpuscles through the Walls of the Vessels, Etc (PMC9799538)
note: Excerpt: 'The white corpuscles, which seem glued to the internal face of the wall of the vessel, depress this wall, lodge in pockets, and spread into surrounding tissues.' 'Climbed out' stands for pressing into the wall and spreading into the tissue. The same page carries Beale's dissent that white cells and pus cells differ.

sentence: White cells climbed out.
claim: By 1867 Cohnheim had confirmed earlier suspicions that in inflammation leukocytes pass through capillary walls into the tissues.
source_title: Julius Cohnheim (Encyclopaedia Britannica, print view)
note: Excerpt: 'by 1867, he confirmed earlier suspicions that the condition results from the passage of leukocytes (white blood corpuscles) through capillary walls and into tissues'. 'Confirmed earlier suspicions', so the film never says he was first. The end card's fact: Augustus Waller, 'Microscopic Observations on the Perforation of the Capillaries by the Corpuscles of the Blood', Philosophical Magazine, November 1846, 29: 397-405 (historyofmedicine.com, Garrison-Morton); '21 years before' is 1867 - 1846 (computed). Whonamedit credits William Addison (1843), so the card says 'saw', not 'first'; PMC10022970 says Waller 'had not the good fortune to attract attention to his discovery'.

sentence: Where tissue is inflamed, the wall turns sticky, and the cell rolls.
claim: Inflammatory signals (such as IL-1 and TNF) make the vessel lining express E-selectin, which is largely inactive on resting endothelium; P-selectin on the endothelium is needed for leukocyte rolling in mice. These lining molecules are what make an inflamed vessel's wall 'sticky' for passing white cells.
source_title: Zhang J, Huang S, Zhu Z, Gatt A, Liu J. E-selectin in vascular pathophysiology. Front Immunol 2024;15:1401399 (mini review; PMC11294169)
note: Excerpts: 'E-selectin remains largely inactive in resting endothelial cells, however, it is consistently expressed in response to inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1) ... or tumor necrosis factor (TNF)'; 'E-selectin is expressed on the activated endothelium, P-selectin is expressed on platelets and the endothelium'; 'P-selectin-/- mice show no leukocyte rolling in vivo'. Review fix: the line now says where the wall turns sticky. It does not say 'only': the same review notes constitutive E-selectin in skin venules (for skin-homing T cells) and in the bone marrow, so some rolling happens without inflammation. 'Inflamed' echoes the change's 'the inflamed tissue' (c6): the tissue does matter, as the signal, not as the source of pus. The rolling itself is c11.

sentence: Where tissue is inflamed, the wall turns sticky, and the cell rolls.
claim: Selectins on the endothelium (the vessel's lining) tether passing leukocytes and make them roll.
source_title: PMC review on selectin and integrin signalling in leukocyte recruitment (PMC4592324)
note: Excerpt: 'Endothelial selectins initiate tethering and rolling of leukocytes.' 'The wall turns sticky' is the endothelial selectins (c27 for why they appear where tissue is inflamed). This step needs no CD18, so in LAD-I (c15, c25) the cells still roll. The search result did not show the article's title, so the source title is descriptive. The rolling-speed note (a mouse figure) is cut from the picture (review fix).

sentence: Then its grips switch on, and it stops.
claim: Signals from engaged selectins and chemokines activate beta-2 integrins on the leukocyte, which mediate slow rolling and arrest.
source_title: PMC review on selectin and integrin signalling in leukocyte recruitment (PMC4592324)
note: Excerpt: 'Signals from engaged selectins and chemokines activate β2 integrins that mediate slow rolling and arrest.' 'Its grips' are the white cell's β2 integrins (built on CD18), which grip ICAM-1 on the wall (Phillipson 2006). Ley 2007 (bible S22): capture, rolling, then arrest. Review fix: 'its own grips' is now 'its grips' ('own' is kept for the whoa); 'its' against 'the wall' still keeps the cell's molecules and the wall's apart.

sentence: It crawls to a seam between two wall cells.
claim: After arrest, neutrophils crawl along the inside of the vessel to distant emigration sites, using the integrin Mac-1 gripping ICAM-1; cells that cannot crawl start to transmigrate close to where they stopped and are slower to get out.
source_title: Phillipson M et al. Intraluminal crawling of neutrophils to emigration sites: a molecularly distinct process from adhesion in the recruitment cascade. J Exp Med 2006;203(12):2569
note: Mouse intravital work. Only the title is verbatim; the rest summarises the abstract. A follow-up Vav1 study says crawling often heads toward a junction between wall cells, and a review (PMC2882030) says Mac-1 crawling moves the cell toward preferred junctions. 'Seam' means an endothelial junction. Mac-1 is itself a β2 integrin, so 'those grips' (c15) covers the crawl too.

sentence: It crawls to a seam between two wall cells.
claim: Most neutrophils leave between two endothelial cells (paracellular); in mouse venules 60-85 µm wide, fewer than 15% went through a single wall cell (transcellular).
source_title: Xia et al. Conditions that promote transcellular neutrophil migration in vivo. Scientific Reports 2024 (PMC11196655)
note: Excerpt: 'less than 15% of neutrophils extravasated transcellularly in WT mice'. A relayed excerpt on the same study gives about 90% paracellular in the mouse cremaster. Mouse data. The line follows this one cell on the usual route and does not say 'all'; a minority go straight through one wall cell (Ley 2007 lists both routes).

sentence: In a rare inherited condition, those grips are faulty.
claim: In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, a rare inherited condition (incidence estimated at about 1 in a million), mutations in the gene for CD18, the shared subunit of the beta-2 integrins, leave those grips missing, too few or not working, so leukocytes cannot migrate out to infection sites; blood white counts are typically high and pus often fails to form.
source_title: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency - StatPearls (point-of-care 24214)
note: Relayed excerpts (the full text is behind registration): 'Leukocytes cannot migrate to infection sites to kill invading microorganisms due to mutations in the CD18 glycoprotein'; counts are typically elevated; 'no pus'. Search summaries of LAD-I reports (e.g. 'Novel ITGB2 Mutation Is Responsible for a Severe Form of Leucocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1', PMC8913115) relate severity to the degree of CD18 deficiency. Review fix: 'faulty', not 'fail' or 'fail to switch on': the grips are absent, too few or defective. 'Those grips' are the β2 integrins of c12-c13. Placed after the crawl so roll, stop, crawl run unbroken; what the faulty cells do is c25. Not named on air; no talk of infection, treatment or immunity (bible §9, Ep 6).

sentence: Cells roll on past.
claim: Neutrophils from a patient with CD18 deficiency (LAD-I) rolled normally along living venules but could not stick or emigrate when stimulated: they roll on instead of stopping.
source_title: von Andrian UH et al. In vivo behavior of neutrophils from two patients with distinct inherited leukocyte adhesion deficiency syndromes. J Clin Invest 1993;91(6):2893-2897
note: Excerpt: 'Neutrophils from a patient suffering from CD18 deficiency showed normal rolling behavior but were incapable of sticking or emigrating upon chemotactic stimulation.' Intravital microscopy. The second patient (no sLeX, a different syndrome) rolled poorly: not this film's condition. The authors: 'both selectin-carbohydrate-mediated initiation of adhesion and subsequent activation-induced beta 2-integrin engagement are essential for the normal function of human neutrophils in vivo.' One patient's cells, so the picture draws one faulty cell rolling past the seam, no crowd (review fix), and the line describes the faulty cells, not every patient (severity varies, c15). 'Cells', not 'white cells' (review fix: fewer repeats). It ends the why on an open loop: if they roll past, how does this one get out?

sentence: This one wedges its nucleus into the seam, making its own door.
claim: Leukocytes breach the vessel lining by inserting lobes of their nucleus into their leading edge at the junction and generating micron-scale gaps themselves, together with local disassembly of the wall cells' actin filaments; the gaps did not need the wall cells to contract.
source_title: Barzilai S et al. Leukocytes Breach Endothelial Barriers by Insertion of Nuclear Lobes and Disassembly of Endothelial Actin Filaments. Cell Reports 2017;18(3):685-699 (DOAJ record)
note: Excerpt: 'Nuclear squeezing involved either preexistent or de novo-generated lobes inserted into the leukocyte lamellipodia ... Gap and pore formation did not require Rho kinase or myosin II-mediated endothelial contractility.' Weizmann coverage: 'Using their nuclei to exert force, they insert themselves between - as well as into - the cells in the vessel walls.' 'Making its own door' pays off c1 and follows the paper's 'leukocytes generate gaps'; the wall's actin also gives way (the title), but it is not drawn (review fix: the whoa keeps only the speed badge and the spine readout). 'This one' answers the why's faulty cells (c25). The nucleus is drawn lobed (3-5 lobes, StatPearls 31353), not voiced. The only 'own' in the film.

sentence: It pours through a gap narrower than itself.
claim: Squeezing leukocyte nuclei open gaps about 4-5 µm wide in the vessel lining, about half to three-fifths of the round neutrophil's 8.3 µm (c3).
source_title: Mechanical barriers for leukocyte transmigration (Alon lab research page, Weizmann Institute of Science)
note: Excerpt: 'Our live imaging and biochemical manipulation of EC actin turnover suggest that the squeezing nuclei of leukocytes generate 4-5 micron wide gaps by collapsing thin EC actin filaments without rupturing the EC actin or vimentin bundles.' The lab's own summary of its work; its Cell Reports paper (Barzilai 2017, c1) says 'Mononuclear and polymorphonuclear leukocytes generate gaps of similar micron-scale size', so neutrophils are included. Computed: 4 / 8.3 = 0.48 and 5 / 8.3 = 0.60. Review fix: the old source only said 'micron-scale'; this one gives a measured width, so 'narrower than itself' stands. The width is voiced as 'narrower than itself' and not shown (the whoa keeps two labels). A review (PMC3605679) has neutrophils (7-8 µm) passing capillaries as narrow as about 2 µm. 'Pours' is the bible's whoa verb.

sentence: Behind it, the seam seals shut.
claim: When a neutrophil crosses between two wall cells, a gap opens in the VE-cadherin junction as it passes and closes again once it is through: in time-lapse imaging of cultured human vessel-lining cells under flow, the gap was closed after full transmigration (by about 265 s in one example), and in another study the crossing took under 5 minutes, with the gap resealing shortly after.
source_title: Alcaide P, Auerbach S, Luscinskas FW. Neutrophil recruitment under shear flow: it's all about endothelial cell rings and gaps. Microcirculation 2009;16(1):43-57 (PMC2726622)
note: Figure 2 legend (excerpt): 'After full transmigration, the VE-Cadherin gap is closed, and ICAM-1 is again uniformly distributed on the apical surface of the endothelial cell' (TNF-α-activated HUVECs, 1 dyne/cm², frames at t = 65, 100 and 265 s). Cross-checks: Gonzalez, Cyrus & Muller, Am J Pathol 2016 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4861767), figure 8 legend: 'A VE-cadherin gap forms just as the PMN cell is in the act of transmigrating, and TEM occurs within 5 minutes, with the gap resealing shortly after.' Kipcke et al., Front Immunol 2025 (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1665264/full): each gap is paired with junction-associated intermittent lamellipodia (JAIL) that locally restore VE-cadherin adhesion. All three are cultured cells, and no in vivo time course turned up in research, so the line states the seal, not its timing, and the 'sped up' badge carries no minutes. Review fix: replaces 'Around it, the wall pulls tight' (Heemskerk 2016's contractile pore, mostly cultured cells), which sat badly with Barzilai's 'no contractility needed' (c1, c16). It claims the seal behind this one cell, not that an inflamed vessel never leaks (c5): in mice, leak and exit run on different VE-cadherin switches (Wessel 2014, c21).

sentence: So pus is mostly white cells from your blood.
claim: Pus is mainly neutrophils, living and dead, with liquefied tissue debris, microbes and fluid; an abscess is a localized collection of it.
source_title: Abscess and phlegmon (Atlas of Head and Neck Pathology, The Ohio State University College of Medicine)
note: Excerpts: an abscess is 'a localized collection of pus' with 'severe inflammation with masses of neutrophils, living and dead, necrotic tissue debris'; 'leukocytes produce proteases that degrade dead tissue and convert it into pus. This process is termed liquefactive necrosis.' Cross-checks: Britannica's suppuration entry (https://www.britannica.com/science/suppuration) describes pus as mostly dead and dying neutrophils with bacteria, cell debris and fluid leaked from the vessels (the search tool's summary, not a verbatim quote); PathologyOutlines (skin abscess) describes a dense infiltrate with many neutrophils and necrotic debris. 'Mostly' covers the debris, microbes and fluid. Review fix: a pathology source replaces Merriam-Webster, and the line now says what pus is before it says where it comes from (c20). Pus is spoken, never shown; nothing is advised.

sentence: So pus is mostly white cells from your blood.
claim: Pus consists mainly of the debris formed by the disintegration of leukocytes that passed out through the capillary walls (Cohnheim's conclusion, as Britannica gives it).
source_title: Julius Cohnheim (Encyclopaedia Britannica, print view)
note: Excerpt: '... and that pus consists mainly of the debris formed by disintegration of these leukocytes.' 'These leukocytes' are the ones that crossed the capillary walls into the tissue (c10), hence 'from your blood'. Stricker argued that some pus cells come from tissue (PMC10004891), which 'mostly' allows for. It answers the change's wrong idea (c6): from the blood, not from the inflamed tissue.

sentence: Each one let itself out.
claim: A white cell triggers its own way out: in mice, leukocytes set off the dephosphorylation of VE-cadherin Tyr731 through the phosphatase SHP-2, which lets AP-2 bind and starts VE-cadherin's endocytosis, opening the junction; and leukocytes generate the gaps themselves, without needing the wall cells to contract.
source_title: Wessel F et al. Leukocyte extravasation and vascular permeability are each controlled in vivo by different tyrosine residues of VE-cadherin. Nat Immunol 2014;15:223-230
note: Excerpt: 'Leukocytes triggered dephosphorylation of Tyr731 via the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, which allowed the adaptin AP-2 to bind and initiate endocytosis of VE-cadherin.' Knock-in mice: the Y731F mutant reduced neutrophil extravasation in the cremaster, while Y685F blocked the rise in permeability instead. With Barzilai 2017 (c1, c16: leukocytes generate the gaps; no endothelial contractility needed). 'Let itself out' is the cell's agency: it gives the signal, and the wall's own machinery undoes the latch; the film does not claim the wall plays no part. 'Each one': the white cells in pus crossed from the blood (c20), by the route the why and the whoa show. Review fix: replaces 'White cells that rolled, stopped, crawled and squeezed out' (a recap, and 'squeezed' contradicted the whoa's wording).

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, your bone marrow made new neutrophils.
claim: The bone marrow makes neutrophils continuously, at a basal rate of about 5 x 10^10 to 10 x 10^10 a day.
source_title: Summers C et al. Neutrophil kinetics in health and disease. Trends Immunol 2010;31(8):318-324 (PMC2930213)
note: Excerpt: 'Neutrophil abundance, coupled with their brief (6-8 h) circulating half life, mandates a basal rate of production by the bone marrow of 5 × 10^10-10 × 10^10 neutrophils/day.' Britannica gives about 100 billion a day for a normal adult. This row carries only the fact of continuous production; the rate depends on the half-life assumed, so the voiced number is c23's floor, which allows for Lahoz-Beneytez 2016's longer half-life. A resting adult's basal rate, not a verdict on any viewer.

sentence: More than ten million.
claim: Even at a low estimate of 1.5 x 10^10 new neutrophils a day (below every estimate here, including those that use the newer, longer blood half-life of about 19 h), the marrow makes about 174,000 a second: more than ten million by 57.6 s into the film, and about 10.7-11.6 million while the line is spoken.
source_title: Lahoz-Beneytez J et al. Human neutrophil kinetics: modeling of stable isotope labeling data supports short blood neutrophil half-lives. Blood 2016;127(26):3431-3438 (PMC4929930)
note: Excerpts: 'Analysis of glucose-labeling data yielded more precise estimates of half-life, 0.79 ± 0.25 days (19 hours)'; the heavy-water data gave 0.77 ± 0.14 days (18.5 h); the abstract gives 13-19 h. Computed: the tally runs at 1.5 × 10^10 / 86,400 s = 173,611 a second, badged 'low estimate'; it passes 10 million at 10,000,000 / 173,611 = 57.6 s; over the planned line (about 61.8-67.0 s) it reads 10.7-11.6 million. Why the floor: Summers 2010's 5-10 × 10^10 a day (c22) rests on a 6-8 h half-life; for the same pool, production scales as 1 / half-life, so at 19 h it is 5 × 10^10 × 6/19 = 1.58 × 10^10 to 10 × 10^10 × 8/19 = 4.2 × 10^10 a day (at 13 h: 2.3-6.2 × 10^10). Cross-check by pool: a mean total blood granulocyte pool of 70 × 10^7 a kg (circulating 31, marginal 39; a 1964 review, 'The kinetics of granulopoiesis in normal man', search excerpt; the measurements are Athens et al. 1961, https://www.jci.org/articles/view/104338) is 4.9 × 10^10 for 70 kg; 4.9 × 10^10 × ln 2 × 24 / 19 = 4.3 × 10^10 a day, or 1.9 × 10^10 for the circulating pool alone. Dancey 1976 (https://www.jci.org/articles/view/108517) counted marrow production at 0.85 × 10^9 a kg a day from the marrow pool and its transit time, about 6.0 × 10^10 for 70 kg, with no blood half-life involved. At the top (10^11 a day, 1,157,407 a second) the line's window reads 71.5-77.5 million. 'More than ten million' holds while the rate is at least 10,000,000 / 61.8 s × 86,400 = 1.40 × 10^10 a day: every estimate above clears it, so it holds under both half-lives. Review fix: replaces 'More than thirty million' (which needed the 6-8 h half-life). 'Tens of millions' was suggested, but the floor's tally reads about 11 million at the line, so the voice says what the screen shows. Re-check after voicing that 'ten million' lands after 57.6 s. The circulating lifespan is not voiced.
